content.text: When an Effect fetches data for the current props, every change starts another request, and the network doesn't promise to answer in order. If each response just calls
, the last one to arrive wins, not the last one you asked for. The fix is the Effect's cleanup: abort the old request, or ignore its result, before the next one starts.

A support agent clicks through the ticket list quickly: ticket 1041, then 1042. The list highlights 1042, but the details panel settles on 1041's customer, and the agent replies to the wrong person. Nothing failed. Both requests returned 200. The request for 1041 hit a slow database query and finished second, and the component accepted whatever arrived last. On the developer's laptop, where the API answers in a few milliseconds and always in order, the bug never happened once.
The belief: loading data in React takes three steps. Start a
, list the id in the dependency array so it fetches again when the id changes, and call
when the response comes back. Add a loading flag and you're done.

It's half right, which is why it's so common. React's docs agree that an Effect is a reasonable place to fetch data that must match what's on screen: the data should follow the current id however it changed, whether by a click, a back button or a link. And the three-step version passes every demo, because local servers are fast and answer in order. What it misses is that the Effect runs once per id, so several requests can be in flight at once, and nothing in those three steps says which response still matters.
Requests don't finish in the order you send them

React's docs use a search box as the example: type "hello" quickly and the response for "hell" can arrive after the one for "hello", so the screen shows results for a query the user no longer has. Two requests raced, and the wrong one finished last. That's a

blocks.title: Two requests in development are not the bug

content.text: With Strict Mode, React runs your Effect, its cleanup, and the Effect again when the component mounts in development, so the Network tab shows two requests. The docs say there's nothing wrong with that: the first run is cleaned up at once, so its response is ignored. In production there's only one. Guarding the fetch with a ref so it runs once hides the missing cleanup instead of fixing it.

Your framework's data fetching or a data library

blocks.title: Make the race happen on purpose

content.text: Throttle the network in your browser's DevTools, or add a random delay to the endpoint on your development server, then click quickly between items. If the screen ever settles on the wrong one, the cleanup is missing or incomplete.

React's docs list more downsides of fetching in Effects: Effects don't run on the server, parents and children that each fetch create network waterfalls, and nothing is cached when the user comes back. They recommend your framework's data fetching, or a client-side cache such as TanStack Query, SWR or React Router 6.4 and later. If you stay with Effects, keep the logic in one custom Hook so it's easy to swap later.
